sentences.text: Scutellosaurus stands as one of the earliest known armored dinosaurs and represents the most basal form identified so far.
This creature possessed an unusually long tail, likely functioning as a counterbalance to its heavily armored body, with the tail occupying two-thirds of the total body length.
Its skin was protected by hundreds of osteoderms, or bony plates, arranged in up to five parallel rows running from the neck to the tail tip, where some plates were flat and others bore holes.
The animal measured about 1.3 meters in length, stood 50 centimeters high, and had a skull measuring approximately 9 centimeters long.
The spine consisted of six or seven neck vertebrae, seventeen or eighteen torso vertebrae, five sacral vertebrae, and roughly sixty tail vertebrae.
The tail was enormous, reaching a length approximately two and a half times that of the vertebrae located in front of the sacrum.
Small, pointed claws on the hands indicate they were not adapted for walking.
Modern views describe the head as moderately elongated with a flat top and a pointed snout when seen from the side.
This species is the most abundant dinosaur known from the Kayenta Formation.
Despite its heavy armor, the protective plates are estimated to have made up only one-tenth of the animal's total body weight.
A large fourth trochanter on the leg served as an attachment for a powerful muscle, suggesting an adaptation for high speed.
The first skeletons were unearthed in June 1971 by David Lawler, who was an intern at the Museum of Northern Arizona.
Additional partial skeletons have been recovered by the Museum of Northern Arizona and the University of California Museum of Paleontology.
The genus name means 'little shield lizard', and the species name 'lawleri' honors David Lawler, the collector of the holotype specimen.
The genus was formally named by Colbert in 1981.
Its long arms suggest it may have fed on all fours.
The mouth contained wide incisors and a row of leaf-shaped, striated cheek teeth adapted for eating plants.
The metatarsals were moderately long with their upper ends closely spaced in a hollow rear arch, typical of a running animal.
In 2008, Richard Butler identified that the anterior iliac laminae extend forward while folding into each other, and the tail consists of at least fifty-eight vertebrae.
Additional distinguishing features were identified in 2020.
Scutellosaurus belongs to the parent group Thyreophora and is classified within the class Ornithischia.
It serves as the nominal genus for the clade Scutellosauridae, a group coined in 1990.
Fossils date from the Hettangian to the Pliensbachian stages, between 201.4 and 184.2 million years ago.
Remains are found in the Kayenta Formation, which is exposed on Navajo Nation land in northern Arizona.

Later researchers doubted Colbert's hypothesis that the animal could walk on all fours, a view based on his original reconstruction of the skull as quite convex and assuming it was a 'primitive' ornithischian.
